name: Duchy of Prussia
info: The duchy formed in 1525 when the Teutonic Order's Prussian lands were secularized under Albert as a Polish fief; the first Protestant state, it passed to Brandenburg and became a kingdom in 1701.

facts.founder: Albert, Duke of Prussia, the last Grand Master of the Teutonic Knights in Prussia
facts.predecessor: State of the Teutonic Order (Monastic Prussia)

t: The duchy became the first Protestant state when Albert, Duke of Prussia, adopted Lutheranism in 1525 and held his lands as a fief of the Polish Crown.
The duchy was inherited by the Hohenzollern electors of Brandenburg in 1618, a personal union known as Brandenburg-Prussia.
Frederick William, the Great Elector, won full sovereignty in the Treaty of Wehlau of 1657, the step that allowed the duchy to become a kingdom in 1701.
dyk: Martin Luther himself urged Albert, at Wittenberg in 1522 and at Nuremberg in 1524, to turn the Teutonic Order's land into a secular principality, and helped broker the deal.
ev: In the Prussian Homage of 10 April, Albert is granted the title Duke of Prussia by King Sigismund I of Poland under the Treaty of Kraków
A peasant rebellion breaks out in Sambia; Albert has the rebels arrested and their leaders executed
Duke Albert founds the Albertina University in Königsberg
In Lublin, Albert Frederick pays homage to Sigismund II, who enfeoffs Joachim II of Brandenburg and his descendants as co-heirs
The duchy passes to the Hohenzollern electors of Brandenburg
In the Treaty of Wehlau, John II Casimir Vasa recognizes Frederick William's full sovereignty over the duchy
Frederick William enters Königsberg with his troops and forces the city to swear allegiance to him
Elector Frederick III of Brandenburg becomes King in Prussia, and the duchy is elevated to a kingdom

sections.foundation:
The duchy grew out of the Monastic Prussia, the territory of the State of the Teutonic Order, which had been a fief of the Polish Crown since the end of the Thirteen Years' War (1454–1466). As Protestantism spread among the laity, dissent grew against the Catholic rule of the Teutonic Knights. Their Grand Master, Albert, of a cadet branch of the House of Hohenzollern, had lost a war against the Kingdom of Poland and lacked the military means to assert the order's authority. His bishop, Georg von Polenz of Pomesania and of Samland, had turned Lutheran in 1523, and Martin Luther urged Albert at Wittenberg in 1522 and at Nuremberg in 1524 to make the land a secular principality.

On 10 April 1525 Albert resigned his office, became a Protestant and, in the Prussian Homage in Kraków, was granted the title Duke of Prussia by his uncle, King Sigismund I of Poland, under the Treaty of Kraków. Back in Königsberg he declared his conversion; only Eric of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, Komtur of Memel, opposed him. On 10 December 1525 the Prussian estates set up the Lutheran Church in Ducal Prussia with the Church Order. The duchy was home to German, Polish (mainly in Masuria) and Lithuanian (mainly in Lithuania Minor) speakers.
sections.socioeconomy:
The nobility changed little in the passage from the monastic state to the duchy, but its control over the dependent peasantry grew. Prussia's free peasants, the Kölmer, held free estates under Culm law with about a sixth of the arable land, much more than in other lands of the feudal era. Taxation by the nobility, the conflicts of the Reformation and the abrupt secularization fed peasant unrest, and a rebellion broke out in Sambia in 1525. Its relatively well-to-do leaders, among them a miller from Kaimen and an innkeeper from Schaaken, demanded a return to the older tax of two marks per hide, a measure of about forty acres.

The Teutonic Order had Christianized the rural population only superficially and built few churches. Old Prussian and Prussian Lithuanian peasants kept pagan customs in places, honouring Perkūnas, Potrimpo and Pikullos; Bishop George banned pagan worship in 1524 and again in 1540. He ordered native languages used at baptisms in 1524, and the rural population of native descent was thoroughly Christianized only with the Reformation. Ducal Prussia became known as a land of Protestantism and sectarianism.
sections.military:
The duchy was born of weakness: Albert had lost a war against Poland and could not defend the order's authority by arms. Under the arrangement with the Polish Crown he nevertheless kept his own army. When the Sambian peasants rose in 1525, saying they were rebelling against the harsh nobility and not the duke, Albert, back from the Holy Roman Empire, called them to a meeting in a field, surrounded them with loyal troops and had them arrested without incident; the leaders were executed, and there were no more large-scale rebellions.

The duchy was drawn into the wars of its neighbours in the 17th century. During the Polish–Swedish wars it was administered from 1635 by the Polish statesman Jerzy Ossoliński. In the Second Northern War Charles X Gustav of Sweden invaded Ducal Prussia and made it a Swedish fief by the Treaty of Königsberg in January 1656. Frederick William, the Great Elector, joined Sweden in the Treaty of Marienburg for the promise of Polish provinces, and the Treaty of Labiau made him full sovereign; he then changed sides for Poland's counteroffer. In 1662 he entered Königsberg with his troops to force the capital's allegiance.
sections.governance:
Administratively little changed from the rule of the Teutonic Knights. Although formally a vassal of the Polish Crown, Albert kept self-government for Prussia, his own army, the minting of his own currency, a provincial assembly (the Landtag) and substantial autonomy in foreign affairs. The Church Order of 1525 made Lutheranism the state church, the first Protestant one, and provided for visitations of parishes, first carried out by Bishop George in 1538; officials toured the duchy enforcing Lutheran teaching and penalizing pagans and dissidents.

When Albert died in 1568 his teenage son Albert Frederick inherited the duchy. Joachim II of Brandenburg won co-enfeoffment for his line, granted at Lublin on 19 July 1569. As Albert Frederick became increasingly feeble-minded, Margrave George Frederick of Brandenburg-Ansbach became regent in 1577. Agreements with Sigismund III in 1605 and the Treaty of Warsaw of 1611 confirmed Brandenburg's claim, in return guaranteeing Catholic worship. George William was invested with the duchy in 1623. Many Junkers opposed Hohenzollern rule from Berlin, and most of society kept the tie with Poland as a safeguard against absolutism.
sections.impact:
As the first Protestant state, established in a deal partly brokered by Luther, Ducal Prussia anticipated the settlement of the Peace of Augsburg of 1555. Albert's marriage on 1 March 1526 to Princess Dorothea, daughter of King Frederick I of Denmark, tied Lutheranism to Scandinavia, and he was aided by his brother George, Margrave of Brandenburg-Ansbach. The Holy Roman Empire and the Catholic Church banned Albert for his Protestantism, and the Teutonic Knights under Walter von Cronberg went on claiming Prussia without success.

In 1544 Albert founded the Albertina University in Königsberg, the main school for the Lutheran pastors and theologians of Prussia. A privilege from Sigismund II Augustus in 1560 gave it the rights of the Kraków University, making it one of the leading universities of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. Because services were held in native languages, Albert appointed exiled Protestant Lithuanian pastors such as Stanislovas Rapolionis and Abraomas Kulvietis as professors, and the Albertina became a centre of Lithuanian language and literature. The duchy's sovereignty under Brandenburg later laid the ground for the Kingdom of Prussia.
sections.decline:
In return for Frederick William's renunciation of the Swedish alliance, King John II Casimir Vasa recognized his full sovereignty over the duchy in the Treaty of Wehlau of 19 September 1657 and the Treaty of Bromberg of 6 November 1657, confirmed in the 1660 Treaty of Oliva. After almost 200 years of Polish suzerainty, the territory passed under the full sovereignty of Brandenburg. The population, whatever its language, resisted, fearing Brandenburg absolutism. The burghers of Königsberg, led by Hieronymus Roth, rejected the treaties and held Prussia to be within the Polish Crown, until Frederick William forced the city's allegiance in 1662. The Polish-French Treaty of Jaworów of 1675 planned a return to Polish suzerainty, but it was never carried out.

Full sovereignty allowed Elector Frederick III of Brandenburg to become King in Prussia in 1701, and the duchy was elevated to a kingdom. After the First Partition of Poland in 1772 the former duchy, with Warmia, was reorganized as the Province of East Prussia. The kingdom and Brandenburg were joined de jure only after the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire in 1806.

summary: The Duchy of Prussia was the secularized state of the Teutonic Order, made a Lutheran duchy under Albert in 1525 as a fief of the Polish Crown. Inherited by the Hohenzollern of Brandenburg in 1618, it won full sovereignty in 1657 against the wishes of many of its people, and in 1701 it became the Kingdom of Prussia.
references: Friedrich, Karin, Brandenburg-Prussia, 1466–1806: The Rise of a Composite State (Palgrave Macmillan, 2011)
